name: Benzoyl peroxide

card.summary: The over-the-counter acne staple with a strong guideline recommendation and decades of trials; the main trade-off is dryness and irritation.
card.aka: BPO, benzoyl peroxide wash or gel (e.g. 2.5%, 5%, 10%)
card.note: Can irritate and dry skin, bleach fabric and hair, and is more irritating when combined with other topical actives.

quick.overview:
Benzoyl peroxide is a topical antibacterial and keratolytic agent sold in washes, creams and gels, mostly for acne. It is available over the counter in several strengths and is also found in prescription combinations with adapalene or clindamycin.

In the 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline it receives a strong recommendation. In looksmaxxing forums it is discussed as a cheap acne product, and some posters also describe using it on the body to reduce odor, a use that has little published support in the published literature.
quick.mechanism: It releases oxygen radicals that act against Cutibacterium acnes, the skin bacterium involved in acne, and it has a peeling (keratolytic) effect that helps unclog pores.
quick.risks: Dryness, peeling, redness and stinging are the most commonly reported effects, and product labels advise that irritation is more likely when another topical acne medicine is used at the same time. It can bleach fabric. Animal studies from 1981 reported tumour-promoting activity in mice under experimental conditions; the clinical relevance is not established in the published literature.

lead: Benzoyl peroxide (BPO) is a topical acne ingredient that helps people get clearer skin by reducing the bacteria, clogged pores and inflamed pimples that make up breakouts. It is sold over the counter as washes, creams, gels and leave-on products, and it also appears in prescription combination products [1][2][29]. It is described as an antibacterial and keratolytic (pore-unclogging, peeling) agent [1], and it is on the World Health Organization Model List of Essential Medicines [29].

The 2024 American Academy of Dermatology acne guideline makes strong recommendations for benzoyl peroxide, topical retinoids, topical antibiotics and oral doxycycline [3]. A JAMA review lists it among first-line topical therapies [4], and a 2022 network meta-analysis of 179 randomized trials found a combined retinoid and benzoyl peroxide to be the most effective topical option assessed for mild-to-moderate acne [6]. Unlike topical antibiotics, benzoyl peroxide is not reported to select for resistant bacteria, which is one reason it is often paired with them [29][30].

In looksmaxxing communities benzoyl peroxide is discussed as a cheap, widely available skin-clearing product, including by people dealing with acne during testosterone or steroid use, and some posters promote benzoyl peroxide washes on the armpits and back as a body-odor measure [22][24][26]. No published trial tests it for odor. Its best-known downsides are dryness, irritation and bleaching of fabric, and since 2024 researchers have also reported that some products can contain or form benzene [29][31][32].

chain: Kills Cutibacterium acnes and loosens clogged pores
Fewer and less inflamed pimples and blackheads
Clearer, more even-looking skin on the face, chest and back
angle.text: Benzoyl peroxide is applied to the skin as a wash or leave-on gel to reduce active acne lesions on the face, chest and back. Clearer skin is the visible payoff; communities also use it alongside other products when hormone use brings breakouts.

paras: Benzoyl peroxide is an organic peroxide made of two benzoyl groups joined by an oxygen-oxygen bond (formula C14H10O4). It is a white granular solid that dissolves poorly in water, and it is also known as dibenzoyl peroxide or BPO [29]. The weak peroxide bond breaks down readily, which underlies both its industrial use as a source of free radicals and its action on skin [29].

Industrially its main use is as a radical initiator for making polymers such as polyesters and PMMA, and for curing rubber and dental cements; it also bleaches flour, hair, plastics and textiles [29]. In dentistry it is used for tooth whitening [29]. In the skin-care aisle it is best known under brand names such as Benzac and PanOxyl [29].

For skin, benzoyl peroxide is used to reduce the pimples, blackheads and red inflamed bumps of acne vulgaris, so that skin looks clearer and more even. Product labels describe it as penetrating pores to help clear and prevent blemishes and blackheads [2]. A Delphi consensus of 62 dermatologists agreed that benzoyl peroxide is among the ingredients recommended for acne and oily skin [5].

Washes are commonly used on the chest, shoulders and back as well as the face. Forum users report using benzoyl peroxide washes on the armpits and back as a 'softmax' to reduce body odor by reducing skin bacteria [22]; published studies do not address that use, and a registered trial of benzoyl peroxide for foot odor was withdrawn [18].

Benzoyl peroxide is used for acne vulgaris alone or in combinations with clindamycin, erythromycin, salicylic acid, sulfur, adapalene or tretinoin [29]. Dermatology literature also lists it among topical options for rosacea and mentions use against seborrheic dermatitis and pitted keratolysis, although the strength of evidence differs between these conditions [13][7][1].
It is also used in clinical settings to reduce skin colonization with Cutibacterium acnes before certain surgeries, as shown by registered trials in shoulder and spine surgery [17][20].

In acne it is classically described as having three effects: killing Cutibacterium acnes through non-specific oxidation, breaking down keratin plugs (comedolytic), and reducing oil production, although evidence for the last is described as disputed [29]. At very low concentrations it has also been reported to stop neutrophils releasing reactive oxygen species, an anti-inflammatory effect [29]. On skin it breaks down into benzoic acid and oxygen [29].

Because it acts through oxidation rather than a single bacterial target, it does not appear to cause bacterial resistance, in contrast to topical antibiotics [29][30]. A systematic review of antibiotic resistance in acne described rising resistance to topical and oral antibiotics [16], which is a reason guidelines discuss combining antibiotics with other agents [3].

US over-the-counter and prescription products are typically 2.5% to 10% in washes, gels, creams or liquids [29]. Wikipedia summaries state that higher concentrations have not been shown to work better but cause more irritation, and that lower concentrations work about as well with fewer side effects [29][30]. Forum users also trade tips on strength, with replies noting that 5% is commonly suggested for the face and 10% for the body [23].

Fixed combinations include adapalene/benzoyl peroxide gel, clindamycin/benzoyl peroxide, and a tretinoin/benzoyl peroxide product approved in the US in 2021 [29]. A phase II trial tested a fixed-dose triple combination of clindamycin, benzoyl peroxide and adapalene in moderate-to-severe acne [10].

A 2022 network meta-analysis of 179 randomized trials with about 35,000 observations found that for mild-to-moderate acne the most effective topical option was a combination of a retinoid with benzoyl peroxide [6]. A 2000 randomized trial of 107 patients compared blue and red light phototherapy with 5% benzoyl peroxide cream and a control light [15].

Phase III trials of adapalene/benzoyl peroxide gel enrolled 1,670 and 452 people with acne vulgaris [21][19]. Older clinical reports from 1966 and 1980 describe benzoyl peroxide, including with sulfur, in acne management [12][11]. In a comparison cited on Wikipedia, azelaic acid produced a lesser treatment response than benzoyl peroxide [30].
Skin-care adjuncts such as ceramide and niacinamide moisturizers have been studied alongside anti-acne treatment for barrier support and tolerability [8][9].

The product label for a benzoyl peroxide cleanser says it is for external use only, warns to avoid the eyes, and states that irritation and dryness are more likely when another topical acne medicine is used at the same time [2]. Redness, burning, dryness, peeling and stinging are the typical effects; they are dose-dependent and tolerance usually develops within a few weeks [1][29].

A true allergic reaction is reported in roughly 1 in 500 people, with burning, itching, crusting and possible swelling, and about a third of people react to UVB light in phototoxicity testing [29]. A 1977 human maximization study found that 76% of subjects became sensitized to 5% and 10% formulations [29]. Forum users describe drying, redness and flaking with leave-on gels and recommend lower strengths for the face [23].

Contact with fabric or hair, including a towel or pillowcase that touched still-moist product, can cause rapid and permanent colour fading [29]. Wikipedia notes that explosion and ignition hazards apply to pure organic peroxides rather than to the concentrations used in cosmetics [29].

In a 1981 mouse study published in Science, benzoyl peroxide promoted skin tumours after prior application of a known initiator and was not active alone as a carcinogen or initiator [14]. A 1999 IARC review found no convincing evidence of skin cancer in humans and classed it in Group 3, not classifiable as to carcinogenicity [29]. The 1981 paper was an animal experiment and did not assess people using acne products.

In 2024 Kucera and colleagues reported in Environmental Health Perspectives that benzoyl peroxide drug products can form benzene [31]. A 2025 paper in the Journal of Investigative Dermatology tested 111 over-the-counter benzoyl peroxide products stored at room temperature and found benzene at 0.16 to 35.30 parts per million. In stability tests on a prescription product, benzene did not appear at 2 degrees C but formed at high levels at 50 degrees C, and in laboratory face-model experiments benzene formed under UV light and was detected in surrounding air [32]. The authors concluded that formation during use may pose significant risk regardless of the starting benzene level [32].

Wikipedia notes that benzene formation occurs above 50 degrees C and cites a United States Pharmacopeia statement on third-party laboratory benzene findings [29]. Storage temperature is the variable the authors highlight, and the study reports that cold storage substantially reduced formation [32].

Sir Benjamin Collins Brodie first prepared benzoyl peroxide in 1858 by reacting benzoyl chloride with barium peroxide [29]. In 1901 Kastle and Loevenhart observed that it released oxygen, and around 1905 Loevenhart reported using it on burns, leg ulcers and tinea sycosis, with low toxicity in animals [29]. It was proposed for wounds in 1929 and for sycosis vulgaris and acne varioliformis in 1934 [29]. One encyclopedic summary dates its acne use to the 1930s [1].

It was officially approved for acne in the US in 1960, although earlier preparations were often of questionable quality [29]. A 1966 report in the Canadian Medical Association Journal discussed benzoyl peroxide with sulfur as a foundation for acne management [12]. A Welsh chemist, Donald Holroyde Hey, inferred that its breakdown produces free phenyl radicals [29]. In 2021 it ranked 284th among prescribed medicines in the US, with more than 700,000 prescriptions [29].

Benzoyl peroxide is available over the counter in the US and as prescription combinations [2][10]. In Australia it is Schedule 5 (Caution) [29]. NIOSH has developed criteria for a recommended workplace standard, and it is listed as the food additive E928 as a flour improver [29].

On looksmax.org, threads ask which strength to buy, with replies noting that 5% is commonly suggested for the face and 10% for the body because leave-on gels can dry skin [23]. One thread frames benzoyl peroxide washes as a 'softmax' for body odor [22].

On T Nation, users discussing acne during testosterone therapy or steroid use mention benzoyl peroxide washes alongside salicylic acid products, sometimes while waiting for a dermatologist's isotretinoin prescription [24][26][27]. Others note that it is less suited to nodular or cystic acne and discuss isotretinoin for that [25]. A 2010 thread on clear skin also lists it among basics [28].

Benzoyl peroxide is commonly used alongside topical retinoids such as adapalene and tretinoin, salicylic acid, azelaic acid and moisturizers, and oral options such as doxycycline or isotretinoin are discussed for more severe acne [3][4][30]. Sunscreen is often advised with acne treatment [30].

lore.intro: Benzoyl peroxide is discussed in these communities as a routine acne product, as a companion to hormone use, and in one prominent thread as a body-odor aid [22][23][24].

claims.claim: Benzoyl peroxide washes reduce body odor.
claims.believers: One poster says it kills the bacteria that break sweat down and recommends a BPO wash on the armpits and back every second or third day [22].
claims.experts: No published study tests it for body odor; a registered foot-odor trial was withdrawn [18].

claims.believers: Forum users treat it as an inexpensive staple, though some describe it as suited to mild acne or whiteheads [23][25][28].
claims.experts: Guidelines give it a strong recommendation and trials show it is effective, especially combined with a retinoid [3][6].

claims.believers: Some posters ask for 10% for quicker results [23].
claims.experts: Wikipedia summaries state that higher concentrations lack strong evidence of greater efficacy and cause more irritation [29][30].

claims.claim: Benzoyl peroxide dries and irritates the skin.
claims.believers: Users report red, flaky skin, especially with leave-on gels [23].
claims.experts: Product labels and dermatology summaries list dryness and irritation as common, particularly with other acne products [2][29].

claims.claim: Benzoyl peroxide is enough for cystic or nodular acne.
claims.believers: Some T Nation posters pair it with washes during hormone-related breakouts, while others say stronger treatment such as isotretinoin is needed for nodular acne [25][27].
claims.experts: Guidelines list it among first-line topical options and also describe retinoids, antibiotics and isotretinoin for other severities [3][4].
